clue.text: Praise daughter acquiring vehicle - using this?

definitions.text: Praise daughter acquiring vehicle - using this?

blocks.note: to credit someone is to praise them; as a noun, credit is praise
a car is a vehicle
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what payment method was used when a daughter bought a car after being praised.
explanation.walkthrough: The daughter acquires the vehicle, so CAR comes before D. The whole clue doubles as the definition: buying a car with a plastic card on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: A plastic payment card lets you borrow to buy things such as a car, which is what the question hints at.

clue.text: Dressed shellfish finally reduced by 50 per cent

indicators.note: the last letter, read as a Roman numeral, is cut to half its value and swapped for the numeral worth that much

blocks.note: a clam is a shellfish
M is 1000 in Roman numerals; half of it is 500, which is D

explanation.surface: A recipe note: shellfish served dressed, its quantity cut in half at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the final M (1000) of CLAM for D (500), halving it.
explanation.definitionFit: Clad is an old past participle of clothe, so it means wearing clothes.

clue.text: Axle he's broken makes a blow-out?

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so these letters are put back together in a new order

blocks.note: the letters used as written

explanation.surface: A car's broken axle seems to have caused a tyre blow-out.
explanation.walkthrough: A blow-out sounds like a burst tyre, which suits the axle; here it is a long breath out.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who breathes out forcefully is literally blowing air out, hence the playful question mark.

clue.text: I'm holding plastic ID valid in US, for independence

indicators.note: plastic material can be moulded into any shape, so these letters can be reshaped
the first piece holds the second inside it, wrapping round it

blocks.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
the letters used as written

explanation.surface: Someone shows a plastic identity card that works in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic ID' reads as an identity card, but plastic is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Individualism is the outlook of self-reliance and personal independence rather than reliance on the group.

clue.text: Council of 100 once gathering in the Italian Vatican's west wing

indicators.note: to gather something is to take it in, so the word placed next takes in what follows
the west wing of a word written left to right is its leftmost part, the opening letter

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
taken as written
la is the feminine form of 'the' in Italian
the opening letter of Vatican

explanation.surface: A council once met inside the western wing of the Vatican palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Italian' needs the feminine article here, not il. Once looks like a time word but is taken literally and wraps the middle pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclave is a private assembly, most famously the gathering of cardinals that elects a pope.

clue.text: One in eight who likes an argument?

definitions.note: a noun phrase in disguise: one who likes a row

blocks.note: first meaning: a member of a racing eight, a crew of eight oarsmen
second meaning, playful: a row (rhymes with cow) is a quarrel

explanation.walkthrough: The same spelling gives two different sounds: the boat sense rhymes with 'go', the quarrel sense with 'cow'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oarsman in an eight pulls an oar, and a made-up noun from row meaning quarrel describes a squabbler.

clue.text: This Italian city's building banks

blocks.note: surface reading: some Italian city is putting up banks
setter's reading: the city's famous building leans, as an aircraft banks when it tilts

explanation.walkthrough: Banks is a verb here, meaning tilts, not a noun for lenders.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tuscan city is world-famous for its leaning bell tower, a building that tilts to one side.

clue.text: Sign one's leading 200 metres, maybe losing the lead

indicators.note: leading means going in front, so this piece comes first
losing its lead means dropping the front letter of the word

blocks.note: one is I, and 'one's' read as 'one is' becomes I'M
the 200 metres is an example of a sprint race

explanation.surface: An athlete one is ahead in the 200 metres but may fade at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: SPRINT drops its first letter to become PRINT.
explanation.definitionFit: An imprint is a mark or sign left behind, as a footprint is an impression in the ground.

clue.text: Partly topless, boxing podcaster showing some nerve

indicators.note: without its top, in a down clue, a word loses its opening letter
to box something is to enclose it as in a box

blocks.note: taken as written
Joe Rogan is a famous podcaster

explanation.surface: A partly bare-chested podcaster tries boxing, which takes some nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: PARTLY loses its P, then the remainder boxes ROGAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting arrogantly means behaving with presumptuous self-importance, which is to show nerve or cheek.

clue.text: Lamps occasionally used to conceal bug

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of the word
hid means concealed; 'to conceal' stands in for its past form here

explanation.surface: Lamps are sometimes rigged to hide a listening device.
explanation.walkthrough: Bug looks like a hidden microphone, which suits the lamps; it is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An aphid is a small sap-sucking insect, and bug is the informal name for any insect.

clue.text: Sapper conceivably appears in publication

blocks.note: surface reading: a soldier from the engineers may get his name in print
setter's reading: the six letters of the word sapper, rearranged, can be found inside the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is NEW followed by SPAPER, an anagram of sapper; conceivably signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily newspaper is a printed periodical, so it is a publication.

clue.text: Mail tags column carried by Times, cheers politicians

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece carried by another sits on top of it, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: a post is an upright column
ages are long times or eras
ta is British slang for thanks
MPs are Members of Parliament

explanation.surface: A newspaper column tags the mail, with Times readers cheering politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mail tags' looks like a headline about the Daily Mail; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Postage stamps are small labels stuck on letters to show postage is paid, a fair description of tags on mail.

clue.text: Some versatile Velcro's singular facility for holding things up

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so the letters sit inside a longer run of words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Velcro is praised as a uniquely versatile fastener for keeping things up.
explanation.walkthrough: Holding things up suits Velcro attaching things, but it means delaying traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: Where a road crosses a railway, barriers come down and halt the cars, so it holds up traffic.

clue.text: India's acted, censoring article poorly

indicators.note: a censor cuts material out, so a piece is removed from the word before it

blocks.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
a is the indefinite article
posed means put on an act or pretended

explanation.surface: India is accused of acting badly by censoring a newspaper article.
explanation.walkthrough: Poorly looks like an adverb modifying acted; in Britain it is an adjective meaning ill.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage, feeling poorly means slightly ill, which is what indisposed means.

clue.text: Steep plunge in numbers - I have to ring editor

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the outer letters go round the inner

blocks.note: NOS is the usual abbreviation for numbers
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
I've, without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A sharp drop in sales figures has to be relayed to the editor by phone.
explanation.walkthrough: NOS and IVE together ring ED: NOS(ED)IVE. Ring looks like a phone call but means surround.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosedive is a steep downward plunge, first of an aircraft and then of prices or numbers.

clue.text: Case of Everton pursuing quick fix

indicators.note: a case is the outside covering, so only the letters at each edge are kept
pursuing means chasing behind, so this piece comes after the other

blocks.note: fast means quick
the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Everton, the Liverpool football club, look for a quick fix for their case.
explanation.walkthrough: Everton is an English Premier League football club from Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten is to fix something firmly in place, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Listener covers EU admitting member France repeatedly seconds

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them in, so the outer pair of letters takes in the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
an arm is a limb, a member of the body
F is the international code for France, given twice
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: Someone listening reports that the EU has let France in again and again in seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener' looks like a person hearing the news; with covers, it is the ear wanting warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: Earmuffs are padded coverings worn over the ears, the listening organs, to keep them warm.

clue.text: Is pub outside Circle line on map?

indicators.note: outside here means beyond, standing past the next piece in the reading order

blocks.note: taken as written
the letter O is round like a circle
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: A tourist asks whether the pub is outside the Circle line on the Tube map.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle line is a London Underground route, which makes 'line on map' look like a Tube line.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line on a weather chart joining places of equal atmospheric pressure.

clue.text: Past inquiry oddly ignored twisted attack

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-numbered positions keeps only the second, fourth and sixth letters
twisted round, the kept letters are turned the other way

blocks.note: over means finished, in the past
the even-placed letters of the word

explanation.surface: A previous investigation strangely brushed aside a vicious assault.
explanation.walkthrough: Oddly ignored means the odd-numbered letters are dropped, not kept.
explanation.definitionFit: To overrun a position is to invade and swamp it, a form of military attack.

clue.text: Sport with graduate facing another in middle of pitch

indicators.note: facing means standing opposite and in front, so this piece leads
a piece set in the middle of a word splits it, the word going round it

blocks.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts graduate
to pitch a product is to try to sell it
another graduate, a second BA

explanation.surface: A sport is played with one graduate facing another in the middle of the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitch looks like a sports field but means a sales pitch, the patter used to make a sale.
explanation.definitionFit: Baseball is the American bat-and-ball game, so it is a sport.

clue.text: Best to date everyone - it uplifted me

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted up means read from bottom to top, the other way round

blocks.note: all means everyone
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone says everyone agreed it was their best moment yet, and it lifted their spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Uplifted only reverses the word right before it; everyone and me stay as they are.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-time record is the best ever achieved up to now, unbeaten to date.

clue.text: Eccentric speculator, I'm hoarding eastern gold?

indicators.note: eccentric means odd and off-centre, so these letters are scrambled
a hoarder keeps a stash inside, so the next piece goes within

blocks.note: the letters used as written
E is the standard abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: An odd investor admits to hoarding gold from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: The E sits among the other letters before they are all rearranged. The question mark marks gold as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold is a rare and valuable metal, a classic example of the category alongside silver and platinum.

clue.text: Become mature, supporting American tradition

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes second

blocks.note: US abbreviates United States, so American
to age is to grow older or mature

explanation.surface: An American tradition lets someone mature in their own time.
explanation.walkthrough: AGE is written under US in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means established custom or practice, the habitual way things are done, much as a tradition is.

clue.text: Get softer, experienced female replaced by male

indicators.note: one letter is taken out and another put in its place

blocks.note: to have felt something is to have experienced it
F is the abbreviation for female
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: An experienced woman is replaced by a man, perhaps one more soft-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: In FELT, the F for female is swapped for M.
explanation.definitionFit: To melt is to soften, whether a solid turning liquid with heat or a heart softening.

clue.text: Player's focus in Moscow: drink some beer!

indicators.note: the focus of something is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of the six-letter name
rum is a spirit drink
a half is a half-pint of beer in a British pub

explanation.surface: A footballer in Moscow is focused on drinking some beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player's' reads as a possessive but is 'player is'. A half is a half-pint glass of beer in British pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrum-half is a rugby player who feeds the ball into the scrum, so a player in a team.

clue.text: State of India embodied by lion's 'crown'

indicators.note: to be embodied by something is to be contained within its body

blocks.note: India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the mane is the crowning hair round a lion's head

explanation.surface: India is personified as a lion wearing a crown.
explanation.walkthrough: State looks like a nation such as India, but India just gives a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is one of the fifty United States, in the far north-east of New England.

clue.text: Hollow tooth doctor extracting first

indicators.note: to extract is to pull out, as a tooth is pulled, so letters are removed

blocks.note: a dentist is a doctor for teeth
first is written 1st, and 1 looks like I

explanation.surface: A dentist pulls a hollow tooth at the first opportunity.
explanation.walkthrough: First looks like an order to take the first letter, but it supplies IST from 1ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A dent is a small hollow pressed into a surface, so the noun fits.

clue.text: Constant factor in drift nets is reptiles rolling around

indicators.note: a factor is a component inside a larger whole, so the letters lie within the words
something rolled round is turned over, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: the run from the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Reptiles caught tumbling in drift nets are a constant problem for fishermen.
explanation.walkthrough: Drift nets are long fishing nets left to drift, which often trap turtles.
explanation.definitionFit: Persistent means continuing without letting up, so constant in the sense of unceasing.
